report.summary: Reviewed chunk 2 of 5 of worktree.py, covering helper functions and the detailed _remove_tree_no_follow with its invariant documentation. No code errors found, but several claims about external callers and tests are uncheckable.
risks: _remove_tree_no_follow | medium | The function's docstring claims that mutation testing shows the suite does NOT go red if the is_dir branch is deleted, but that claim is uncheckable without the test suite. | Review the mutation test results or run the test suite with that branch removed.

_remove_tree_no_follow | low | The docstring mentions '2026-07-28' as a date for a fix, which is in the future, suggesting a possible error in the code. | Verify the intended date or correct the annotation.
todos: Confirm mutation test coverage for the is_dir branch in _remove_tree_no_follow.
Consider hoisting _chain_between out of the per-child loop to optimize depth scaling.

handoff.purpose: Define helper functions for file removal and the core recursive deletion function _remove_tree_no_follow with extensive invariant documentation.

symbols.name: _clear_readonly
symbols.note: Drops the read-only bit on a path, best effort.

symbols.name: _unlink_reparse_point
symbols.note: Removes a reparse point (symlink or junction) without touching its target.

symbols.name: _force_unlink
symbols.note: Unlinks a file, clearing read-only if necessary.

symbols.name: _force_rmdir
symbols.note: Removes a directory, clearing read-only if necessary.

symbols.name: _chain_between
symbols.note: Returns a list of path components from root to target, raises ValueError if root not ancestor.

symbols.name: _remove_tree_no_follow
symbols.note: Recursively deletes a directory tree without following reparse points, with verification at each step.

claims.text: Drop the read-only bit git sets on loose objects, best effort.
claims.why: The function calls os.chmod to set S_IWRITE and S_IREAD, catching OSError.

claims.text: Remove the LINK itself. Never touches what it points at.
claims.why: The function uses os.rmdir or os.unlink to remove the link itself.

claims.text: A directory symlink / junction is removed with ``rmdir``, a file symlink with ``unlink``; which one applies differs by platform and link kind, so both are tried.
claims.why: The function tries os.rmdir first, then os.unlink.

claims.text: ``[root, ..., target]``: every component ``target`` is reached THROUGH.
claims.why: The function builds a chain from target up to root and reverses it, so it includes all components from root to target.

claims.text: Walked upward by comparison KEY rather than with ``relative_to``, which is case-sensitive and would raise on Windows for a differently-cased spelling.
claims.why: The function uses _key(current) comparison, but _key is not defined in this chunk; its behavior regarding case sensitivity is uncheckable.

claims.text: Raises ``ValueError`` if ``root`` is not on ``target``'s path.
claims.why: The function raises ValueError if parent == current (i.e., reached root without matching).

claims.text: Recursively delete ``root`` without ever traversing a reparse point.
claims.why: The function checks for reparse points before acting and uses _unlink_reparse_point for them.

claims.text: EVERY path handed to a syscall that RESOLVES it -- ``os.scandir``, ``os.rmdir``, ``os.unlink``, ``os.chmod`` -- is re-classified with a FRESH ``lstat`` IMMEDIATELY beforehand, together with every component above it, up to and including ``guarded_ancestors``. There are exactly three such sites (the scan, the per-child unlink, the rmdir drain) and all three verify.
claims.why: The chunk shows the scan and per-child unlink verification sites, but the rmdir drain is not in this chunk.

claims.text: No path in this function is acted on twice on the strength of one check.
claims.why: The code shows verification before each action (pop, per-child, and presumably drain).

claims.text: That re-check is the entire fix, and its absence was a live repository-deletion bug -- twice, in the same function, for the same reason.
claims.why: The bug history is not verifiable from this code chunk alone.

claims.text: Three shapes of the same defect, all measured on this box with a live process in the tree swapping an already-classified directory for a junction, three trials each: ...
claims.why: The measurement results are not verifiable from this code.

claims.text: ``shutil.rmtree`` is safe against a junction that is already in place and unsafe against one that appears mid walk; this function is safe against both.
claims.why: Comparison with shutil.rmtree behavior is not verifiable from this code.

claims.text: The few microseconds between each fresh ``lstat`` and the ONE syscall that follows it. Closing even that needs handle-relative traversal (``openat``/``O_NOFOLLOW``), which CPython does not expose on Windows
claims.why: The availability of openat/O_NOFOLLOW on Windows is not verifiable from this code.

claims.text: It is "one verification, one syscall", repeated N times -- not "two adjacent syscalls"
claims.why: The code verifies before each syscall (e.g., _verify_reachable before os.unlink).

claims.text: The EXCEPTIONS TO "ONE VERIFICATION, ONE SYSCALL", NAMED PRECISELY: ... * :func:`_force_unlink` / :func:`_force_rmdir` on ``PermissionError``: ``unlink`` -> ``chmod`` -> ``UNLINK AGAIN`` ... * :func:`_unlink_reparse_point`: ``rmdir`` -> ``unlink`` -> ``chmod`` -> ``unlink``
claims.why: The code for _force_unlink, _force_rmdir, and _unlink_reparse_point matches the described sequences.

claims.text: Re-verifying inside the retry was CONSIDERED AND NOT DONE this round: ``_verify_reachable`` is a closure over the walk's ``root`` and ``guarded_ancestors``, so threading it into these four module-level helpers is a signature change to the primitives, and a guard added without a test that can kill it is exactly what this file has been punished for. It is follow-up #2 behind the hoisting below.
claims.why: The module-level helpers do not call _verify_reachable, confirming the decision.

claims.text: THE COST SCALES WITH DEPTH
claims.why: Performance measurements are not verifiable from this code.

claims.text: At depth 2-3, verifying before every syscall roughly doubles the walk. Median of 3, this box, alternating runs on freshly built identical trees: ...
claims.why: Performance measurements are not verifiable from this code.

claims.text: Against DEPTH, 400 files at the leaf, median of 3, baseline = this same walker with the verification stubbed out entirely, so the only difference measured is the verification: ...
claims.why: Performance measurements are not verifiable from this code.

claims.text: The cost is NOT dominated by the ``lstat`` calls (roughly 5k of them in the 1280-file case, tens of milliseconds) but by rebuilding the lexical chain in Python for every child, which is O(depth) per child
claims.why: The code calls _chain_between for each child, which is O(depth).

claims.text: the available optimisation, named rather than taken: the chain is PURE TEXT, so hoisting ``_chain_between`` out of the per-child loop would recover most of it WITHOUT weakening the invariant
claims.why: The code currently calls _chain_between per child; hoisting is not implemented.

claims.text: Raises ``OSError`` on failure and :class:`WorktreeRemovalRace` if a reparse point appears above ANY step -- the scan, the unlinks, or the drain. A partial delete is reported, never swallowed. That sentence was false as written until 2026-07-28: the drain had no verification, so a partial delete THROUGH a swapped ancestor was neither detected nor reported, and ``cleanup_worktree`` returned normally on top of it.
claims.why: The drain verification is not in this chunk, and the date is ambiguous.

claims.text: A reparse point strictly above ``target`` redirects it wholesale, and unlinking that ancestor would delete a link the manager does not own, so this refuses instead of repairing.
claims.why: The function raises WorktreeRemovalRace if a reparse point is found in the ancestors.

claims.text: Does it exist at all? That is the only question answered here. Whether a path is a reparse point, a file, or a directory is decided in exactly ONE place -- when it is POPPED, immediately before it is opened -- and the root is not special-cased.
claims.why: The code calls os.lstat(root) only to check existence, and classification happens in the pop loop.

claims.text: An earlier version classified the root here as well as in the loop; mutation testing showed the extra branch could be deleted without any test noticing, because the pop-time check already covers it.
claims.why: Mutation test results are not verifiable from this code.

claims.text: RE-CHECK 1 OF 3 (the others are in the entry loop and the drain, and each one is separately load-bearing -- see the mutation notes).
claims.why: The code shows verification at pop (line: _verify_reachable(current)) and per child (line: _verify_reachable(child)). The drain is not in this chunk.

claims.text: What this one specifically stops, measured: a swap of an ancestor AFTER `current` was queued, which sends the not-a-directory branch below into an os.unlink outside the tree.
claims.why: The measurement is not verifiable from this code.

claims.text: RE-VERIFIED PER CHILD, not once per directory. `entries` can be thousands long, and `current` can be renamed aside and a junction renamed into its place between any two iterations -- a rename does not require the directory to be empty, so that swap is available to a live candidate at every moment of this loop.
claims.why: The code calls _verify_reachable(child) for each child inside the for loop.

claims.text: A FRESH lstat, deliberately not entry.stat(): on Windows the DirEntry's stat is served from this scandir's cache (measured), so asking the DirEntry would re-introduce the stale read.
claims.why: The behavior of DirEntry.stat on Windows is not verifiable from this code.

claims.text: HONEST NOTE ON THIS BRANCH: mutation testing shows the suite does NOT go red if it is deleted, and that is not an oversight in the tests -- it is redundant on this platform, measured both ways. A junction is reported as a directory by is_dir(follow_symlinks=False), so it would be queued and then unlinked by the pop-time check; a directory symlink is NOT, so it would fall to _force_unlink, and os.unlink removes a Windows directory symlink without following it (measured: link gone, target intact).
claims.why: Mutation test results and platform-specific behavior measurements are not verifiable from this code.

observations.what: The docstring for _remove_tree_no_follow contains an extensive performance analysis and historical bug description, but the actual code for the drain verification is not in this chunk.
The date '2026-07-28' appears in the docstring, which is in the future relative to the current date, possibly a typo or placeholder.
The function _chain_between uses _key for comparison, but _key is not defined in this chunk, making its behavior unverifiable.
The module-level helpers (_force_unlink, _force_rmdir, _unlink_reparse_point) do not verify the path again before retrying, as noted in the docstring.
